blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html:
Bayes’ theorem reverses the direction of a conditional probability:

P(A|B) = P(B|A) × P(A) ÷ P(B),

where the denominator, by the law of total probability, is P(B) = P(B|A)P(A) + P(B|not A)P(not A).

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: A diagnostic test is validated in people whose true status is known, so it gives you P(positive | disease). The clinician facing a patient with a positive result wants the reverse, P(disease | positive). Bayes’ theorem converts one into the other. It needs one extra ingredient: the probability of disease before the test, called the prior or pre-test probability. In a screening programme that is the prevalence. The answer, P(disease | positive), is the posterior or post-test probability.

blocks.label: Derivation
blocks.html:
The general multiplication rule (§5.3) gives P(A and B) two ways:

P(A|B) × P(B) = P(A and B) = P(B|A) × P(A).

Divide both sides by P(B):

P(A|B) = P(B|A) × P(A) ÷ P(B).

Expand P(B) by the law of total probability. With A = disease (D) and B = positive test (T+):

P(D|T+) = P(T+|D)P(D) ÷ [P(T+|D)P(D) + P(T+|not D)P(not D)].

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html:
A screening test has P(T+|D) = 0.95 and P(T+|not D) = 0.10. In a community where P(D) = 0.01:

  1. Numerator: 0.95 × 0.01 = 0.0095.
  2. Denominator: 0.0095 + 0.10 × 0.99 = 0.0095 + 0.099 = 0.1085.
  3. P(D|T+) = 0.0095 ÷ 0.1085 = 0.088.

Fewer than 9 in 100 people who test positive have the disease. The test is not poor. The healthy pool is 99 times larger than the diseased pool, so its 10% false-positive rate produces far more positives (0.099) than the diseased group’s 95% (0.0095). §5.5.2 repeats this calculation as a table of 10,000 people.

points.html: P(disease | positive) = P(positive | disease) × P(disease) ÷ P(positive), with P(positive) expanded over the diseased and the healthy.
The prior dominates. The same test gives very different post-test probabilities in mass community screening and in a referral clinic (§5.5.2).
Sensitivity and specificity (§5.5.1) are the inputs, predictive values (§5.5.2) are the outputs, and likelihood ratios (§5.5.3) are the same theorem written in odds.

blocks.html: Sensitivity and Specificity

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: Sensitivity (Se) is the probability that the test is positive in a person who has the disease: Se = P(T+|D). Specificity (Sp) is the probability that the test is negative in a person who does not: Sp = P(T−|not D). Both are judged against a reference standard (the best available method for deciding true disease status).

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html:
The results of a test against the reference standard fill a 2×2 table:

Disease present Disease absent
Test positive a (true positives, TP) b (false positives, FP)
Test negative c (false negatives, FN) d (true negatives, TN)

Sensitivity reads down the first column: Se = a ÷ (a + c). Specificity reads down the second: Sp = d ÷ (b + d). Each is a conditional probability given true status, which is exactly what Bayes’ theorem takes as input.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: A new TB screening tool is applied to a consecutive series of 400 adults with cough at a district hospital, and all are also tested with the reference standard. Of 100 with TB, 95 test positive: Se = 95/100 = 95%. Of 300 without TB, 270 test negative: Sp = 270/300 = 90%. The 5 missed cases are false negatives; the 30 TB-free people who tested positive are false positives.

points.html: Se = TP ÷ (TP + FN) measures how well the test catches disease. A highly sensitive test suits initial screening, where a missed case is costly.
Sp = TN ÷ (TN + FP) measures how well it clears the healthy. A highly specific test suits confirmation, where a false positive leads to harmful further intervention.

Se and Sp do not depend on prevalence through the arithmetic (each is computed within one column). They are still not fixed properties of the test. They vary with disease severity, case mix and setting (“It is now well established that sensitivity and specificity are not fixed test properties”, Bossuyt et al., 2015), and a systematic review found consistent effects of disease prevalence and severity on accuracy estimates (Whiting et al., 2013).

Design matters. Non-consecutive inclusion inflates accuracy estimates, and studies that compared severe cases with healthy controls (“two-gate” or case-control sampling) gave the highest estimates of all, though imprecisely (Rutjes et al., 2006); a later systematic review found consistent evidence of an effect of case-control design (Whiting et al., 2013). The preferred design enrols one consecutive or random series of people in whom the test would be used, and classifies all of them by the reference standard; the STARD reporting guideline asks authors to state “whether participants formed a consecutive, random, or convenience series” (Bossuyt et al., 2015).

The exam mnemonics SnNout (a highly sensitive test, when negative, rules out) and SpPin (a highly specific test, when positive, rules in) are shortcuts, and they carry a published “note of caution” (Pewsner et al., 2004). The arithmetic shows why. A test with Se 95% but Sp only 10% is negative in 5% of the diseased and in only 10% of the healthy, so a negative result is merely half as likely in the diseased: it barely rules anything out despite the high sensitivity (in the language of §5.5.3, LR− = 0.05 ÷ 0.10 = 0.5). Judge rule-in and rule-out with the likelihood ratios of §5.5.3.
Moving a test’s cut-off trades sensitivity against specificity. The full trade-off curve is the ROC curve (the plot of sensitivity against 1 − specificity over all cut-offs, §15.5.1).

blocks.html: Positive and Negative Predictive Value

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: The positive predictive value is PPV = P(D|T+), the probability that a person who tests positive has the disease. The negative predictive value is NPV = P(not D|T−), the probability that a person who tests negative is disease-free.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: Sensitivity and specificity answer “given true status, how does the test behave?”. A clinician holds a result and wants the reverse. PPV and NPV read across the rows of the 2×2 table: PPV = a ÷ (a + b), NPV = d ÷ (c + d). They are the outputs of Bayes’ theorem, and because the rows mix diseased and healthy people, they depend on how many of each there are, that is, on prevalence.

blocks.label: Worked Calculation: the 2×2 table for 10,000 people
blocks.html:
Se = 95%, Sp = 90%, prevalence 1% (the example of §5.5).

  1. Diseased: 1% of 10,000 = 100. True positives = 0.95 × 100 = 95; false negatives = 5.
  2. Healthy: 9,900. True negatives = 0.90 × 9,900 = 8,910; false positives = 990.
Disease present Disease absent Total
Test positive 95 990 1,085
Test negative 5 8,910 8,915
Total 100 9,900 10,000
  1. PPV = 95 ÷ 1,085 = 8.8%. The row total 1,085 ÷ 10,000 = 0.1085 is P(T+) from the law of total probability.
  2. NPV = 8,910 ÷ 8,915 = 99.94%.

Of every 1,085 positives, 990 (91%) are false alarms. The table and the formula of §5.5 give the same answer because the table is the formula written out in people.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example: PPV against prevalence
blocks.html:
The same test (Se 95%, Sp 90%) used in different settings:

Setting (illustrative) Prevalence PPV NPV
Mass community screening 1% 8.8% 99.94%
Screening a high-risk group 5% 33.3% 99.71%
PHC, people with symptoms 10% 51.4% 99.39%
Referral clinic 30% 80.3% 97.67%
Specialist clinic 50% 90.5% 94.74%

blocks.alt: PPV and NPV against prevalence for a test with sensitivity 95% and specificity 90%
blocks.caption: Figure 5.2. The same test gives a PPV of 8.8% at 1% prevalence, 51.4% at 10% and 80.3% at 30%. NPV falls slowly as prevalence rises.

blocks.label: Worked Calculation: two tests in series and in parallel
blocks.html:
Test A (Se 0.95, Sp 0.90) and test B (Se 0.80, Sp 0.95), assuming the two tests err independently of each other within the diseased and within the healthy (conditional independence).

Series (call positive only if both are positive; in practice, run B only on A-positives):

  1. Se(series) = Se_A × Se_B = 0.95 × 0.80 = 0.76.
  2. Sp(series) = 1 − (1 − Sp_A)(1 − Sp_B) = 1 − 0.10 × 0.05 = 0.995.

Parallel (call positive if either is positive):

  1. Se(parallel) = 1 − (1 − Se_A)(1 − Se_B) = 1 − 0.05 × 0.20 = 0.99.
  2. Sp(parallel) = Sp_A × Sp_B = 0.90 × 0.95 = 0.855.

At 1% prevalence, series testing gives 76 true and 49.5 false positives per 10,000 (PPV 60.6%, up from 8.8% for A alone), but misses 24 of every 100 cases. Parallel testing catches 99 of 100 cases (NPV 99.99%) at the price of 1,435.5 false positives (PPV 6.5%).

points.html: PPV = TP ÷ (TP + FP); NPV = TN ÷ (TN + FN). Both depend on prevalence; Se and Sp do not, arithmetically.
As prevalence rises with Se and Sp fixed, PPV rises and NPV falls. Reason it through: more of the people tested are diseased, so more positives are true and more negatives are missed cases.
A PPV reported from a hospital study does not transfer to community screening. Recompute it for your own prevalence with Bayes’ theorem or a 2×2 table.

Series testing raises specificity and PPV and lowers sensitivity; parallel testing raises sensitivity and NPV and lowers specificity. The formulas assume conditional independence. Two tests that detect the same feature tend to err on the same people, and then the gains are smaller than the formulas predict.

blocks.html: Likelihood Ratios

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html:
The odds of an event are its probability divided by the probability that it does not happen: odds = p ÷ (1 − p) (recall §1.5). Conversely, p = odds ÷ (1 + odds). A likelihood ratio compares how probable a test result is in people with the disease and in people without it:

LR+ = P(T+|D) ÷ P(T+|not D) = Se ÷ (1 − Sp)

LR− = P(T−|D) ÷ P(T−|not D) = (1 − Se) ÷ Sp

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: Odds and probability describe the same uncertainty on different scales. A probability of 0.2 is odds of 0.2 ÷ 0.8 = 0.25 (“1 to 4”); a probability of 0.5 is odds of 1. Odds are not probabilities: odds can exceed 1, and the two scales agree closely only when p is small. The reason to switch scales is that on the odds scale Bayes’ theorem becomes a single multiplication: post-test odds = pre-test odds × likelihood ratio. Because the LR is built only from Se and Sp, one number summarises the test and can be applied to any patient’s pre-test probability.

blocks.label: Derivation
blocks.html:
Write Bayes’ theorem for D and for “not D”, given a positive result. Both share the denominator P(T+):

P(D|T+) = P(T+|D)P(D) ÷ P(T+)

P(not D|T+) = P(T+|not D)P(not D) ÷ P(T+)

Divide the first line by the second. P(T+) cancels:

P(D|T+) ÷ P(not D|T+) = [P(T+|D) ÷ P(T+|not D)] × [P(D) ÷ P(not D)]

The left side is the post-test odds, the first bracket is LR+, and the second is the pre-test odds. The same steps for a negative result give post-test odds = pre-test odds × LR−.

blocks.label: Worked Calculation: closing the loop with §5.5.2
blocks.html:
Se 0.95, Sp 0.90, pre-test probability 1%.

  1. LR+ = 0.95 ÷ 0.10 = 9.5. LR− = 0.05 ÷ 0.90 = 0.056 (a negative result divides the odds by 18).
  2. Pre-test odds = 0.01 ÷ 0.99 = 0.0101.
  3. After a positive result: post-test odds = 0.0101 × 9.5 = 0.0960; post-test probability = 0.0960 ÷ 1.0960 = 0.088. This is the PPV of the 2×2 table.
  4. After a negative result: post-test odds = 0.0101 × 0.056 = 0.00056; probability of disease = 0.00056, so NPV = 99.94%, again as in the table.
  5. The same positive result in a referral clinic with pre-test probability 30%: odds 0.30 ÷ 0.70 = 0.4286; × 9.5 = 4.071; probability = 4.071 ÷ 5.071 = 0.803.

The LR did not change between settings; only the pre-test odds did.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example: Youden’s index
blocks.html: Youden’s index J = Se + Sp − 1 summarises a test in one number (Youden, 1950). J = 0 for a test no better than chance (then Se = 1 − Sp and LR+ = 1); J = 1 for a perfect test. For the test above J = 0.95 + 0.90 − 1 = 0.85; for test B of §5.5.2, J = 0.80 + 0.95 − 1 = 0.75. For a test measured on a continuous scale, the cut-off that maximises J is one common way to choose a positivity threshold on the ROC curve (§15.5.1). J weights a false negative and a false positive equally, which is rarely true clinically.

points.html: odds = p ÷ (1 − p); p = odds ÷ (1 + odds). Post-test odds = pre-test odds × LR.
LR+ = Se ÷ (1 − Sp); LR− = (1 − Se) ÷ Sp. An LR of 1 means the result does not change the probability of disease.

A widely used rough guide, from the Evidence-Based Medicine Working Group’s users’ guides, treats LRs above 10 or below 0.1 as generating “large and often conclusive changes” in post-test probability, 5–10 and 0.1–0.2 as moderate, and 2–5 and 0.2–0.5 as small (Bhandari et al., 2003, citing Jaeschke et al., 1994). It is a convention: whether a shift is “conclusive” depends on where the pre-test probability starts. An LR+ of 9.5 still left a 1% prior at only 8.8%.
LRs are portable across prevalence only to the extent that Se and Sp are, and §5.5.1 showed they vary with spectrum and setting.
Odds reappear as the basis of the odds ratio (the ratio of odds in two groups, §10.6.4) and logistic regression (§13.2).

questions.prompt: A screening test has excellent sensitivity and specificity but is used in a population with very low prevalence. Explain why most positive results could still be false alarms.
questions.answer: The healthy group is far larger than the diseased group. Even a small false-positive rate, applied to that large group, produces more false positives in absolute numbers than the small diseased group produces true positives. At 1% prevalence with Se 95% and Sp 90%, 990 of 1,085 positives per 10,000 people (91%) are false.

questions.prompt: The test of §5.5 (Se 95%, Sp 90%) is used in a PHC where 10% of those tested have the disease. Build the 2×2 table for 10,000 people and find the PPV. Then get the same answer with pre-test odds and LR+.
questions.answer:
Diseased 1,000: TP = 0.95 × 1,000 = 950, FN = 50. Healthy 9,000: TN = 0.90 × 9,000 = 8,100, FP = 900.

Disease No disease Total
Positive 950 900 1,850
Negative 50 8,100 8,150
Total 1,000 9,000 10,000

PPV = 950 ÷ 1,850 = 51.4% (NPV = 8,100 ÷ 8,150 = 99.4%).

Odds route: pre-test odds = 0.10 ÷ 0.90 = 0.111. LR+ = 0.95 ÷ 0.10 = 9.5. Post-test odds = 0.111 × 9.5 = 1.056. Post-test probability = 1.056 ÷ 2.056 = 0.514, the same PPV.

questions.prompt: Why can a likelihood ratio be carried from one setting to another when a PPV cannot? What limits that portability?
questions.answer: The LR is built only from Se and Sp, each computed within one true-status group, so the arithmetic contains no prevalence; you apply it to any setting’s pre-test odds. The PPV is the output of Bayes’ theorem for one particular prevalence and must be recomputed for another. The limit: Se and Sp themselves vary with disease spectrum, severity and setting (Whiting et al., 2013; Bossuyt et al., 2015), so an LR from a referral hospital may not hold in community screening.
